session.session.moonStrongImpact: Attention : très éclairée et au-dessus de l'horizon, elle peut fortement réduire le contraste des galaxies, nébuleuses et météores faibles
session.session.moonModerateImpact: À noter : son éclairage peut réduire le contraste des objets faibles, surtout près de la Lune
session.session.moonModerateImpact2: Influence généralement modérée ; privilégiez les objets brillants et observez les objets faibles loin de la Lune

session.goalDiscoveryAdvice: Spot the Big Dipper, then extend the alignment of the two stars on the edge of the saucepan up to Polaris. It is a good first exercise to orient yourself in the sky.
session.goalStarsAdvice: Compare the W shape of Cassiopeia with the Big Dipper, then look for Polaris between the two regions of the sky. Take the time to connect the brightest stars of each figure.
session.goalMoonPlanetsAdvice: Start with the Moon if it is present: observe the boundary between lunar day and night, where reliefs stand out well. Then, check in Celestial Atlas which planets are above the horizon at the chosen time.
session.goalGalaxiesAdvice: Try the Andromeda galaxy (M31, especially interesting under a dark autumn sky) or the Orion nebula (M42, winter target). Use binoculars first if you have them; a telescope requires a dark sky and low magnification.
session.goalAstroAdvice: To start, photograph the Moon with a phone held firmly or a camera on a tripod. If the Moon is absent, try a star field with a short exposure, then gradually increase exposure time while watching for trails.

visibleNow.helpText: The selection favours objects above 10° and suggests a few targets according to their type and catalogue magnitude. The 'Spotting' label is an educational estimate based on height, type, magnitude and chosen equipment, not a guarantee of visibility. Light pollution, transparency, surface brightness and experience change the result; diffuse objects can be difficult even with a favourable integrated magnitude. When calculable, culmination indicates when the target passes highest in the sky.
visibleNow.disclaimer: Visibility depends on the location and date selected. Presence above the horizon does not guarantee that the object is visible to the naked eye.

ui.glossaryTerms: Apparent magnitude: apparent brightness (the smaller the number, the brighter the object). RA and declination: coordinates locating the object on the celestial sphere. Azimuth: direction on the horizon, counted from north toward east. Altitude: height above the horizon (0° at the horizon, 90° at the zenith). Seeing (turbulence): atmospheric agitation that blurs details. Transparency: sky clarity; haze, dust and humidity attenuate faint objects.
ui.factMercury: Mean diameter: 4,879 km. Extremely thin atmosphere; heavily cratered surface.
ui.factVenus: Mean diameter: 12,104 km. Very dense atmosphere, mostly CO₂.
ui.factEarth: Mean diameter: 12,742 km. Liquid water on the surface and nitrogen- and oxygen-rich atmosphere.
ui.factJupiter: Mean diameter: about 139,820 km. Gas giant with many moons and cloud bands.
ui.factSaturn: Mean diameter: about 116,460 km. Gas giant famous for its ring system.
ui.factUranus: Mean diameter: about 50,724 km. Ice giant with a strongly tilted rotation axis.
ui.factNeptune: Mean diameter: about 49,244 km. Ice giant with very fast winds.
ui.factSun: Diameter: about 1.39 million km. G2 V type star, photospheric temperature near 5,780 K.
ui.factMoon: Diameter: about 3,475 km. Its surface keeps many impact craters.
ui.suggestUseStarAsLandmark: Use this star as a landmark to understand the stars around it.
ui.factMars: Mean diameter: 6,779 km. Thin atmosphere and surface marked by volcanoes and canyons.
ui.suggestBrightLandmarkAdvice: Take the time to find it with the naked eye and get familiar with the direction.
ui.suggestRecognizeStar: Recognize a star or a shape
ui.suggestRecognizeStarAdvice: Use this star as a landmark to understand the stars around it.
ui.suggestHarderTargetAdvice: Observe first without an instrument; binoculars can help. A diffuse target may remain invisible if the sky is bright.

walk.polarisIntro: The Big Dipper serves as a signpost. You don't need to know the stars by name to begin.
walk.polarisStep1: Find the Big Dipper: it looks like a large saucepan with a handle.
walk.polarisStep2: Find the two stars on the edge opposite the handle: Merak and Dubhe. Extend the line from Merak toward Dubhe, then continue beyond Dubhe about five times their separation.
walk.polarisStep3: You arrive near Polaris. It marks approximately celestial north and is at the end of the handle of the Little Dipper, more discreet.
walk.polarisTip: The Big Dipper and Polaris are circumpolar from metropolitan France: they generally remain above the horizon.
walk.summerIntro: Three very bright stars draw a large triangle in the sky of late spring and summer evenings.
walk.summerStep1: Look for Vega, very bright and almost white-blue. It is in the small constellation of Lyra.
walk.summerStep2: Spot Deneb further to the northeast, in Cygnus, whose stars draw a large cross.
walk.summerStep3: Find Altair to the south of the triangle, in Aquila. Vega, Deneb and Altair together form the Summer Triangle.
walk.summerTip: The triangle is especially practical in summer and early autumn; its height depends on the time and season.
walk.orionIntro: Orion is one of the easiest silhouettes to learn, especially on winter evenings.
walk.orionStep1: Spot three stars fairly close together and almost aligned: this is Orion's belt.
walk.orionStep2: Above and to the left of the belt, look for Betelgeuse, often recognizable by its orange tint.
walk.orionStep3: On the other side, Rigel shines with a white-blue glow. The belt, Betelgeuse and Rigel allow you to find the hunter's silhouette.
walk.orionTip: Orion is especially visible in the evening during late autumn and winter.
walk.pleiadesIntro: The Pleiades are a tight small group of stars that resembles a tiny ladle or a small sparkling cloud.
walk.pleiadesStep1: Start by spotting the constellation Taurus or the bright Aldebaran, with its orange appearance.
walk.pleiadesStep2: Look a little further for a small compact packet of several bluish stars: these are the Pleiades, also called the Seven Sisters.
walk.pleiadesStep3: Observe them first with the naked eye. With binoculars, many more stars appear in the same field.
walk.pleiadesTip: The Pleiades are particularly easy to observe on autumn and winter evenings. They remain an extended object: avoid looking for them with high magnification.
walk.andromedaIntro: M31 is a neighboring galaxy to ours. Under a dark sky, it appears to the naked eye as a small blurry patch, not as a sharp star.
walk.andromedaStep1: Spot the Great Square of Pegasus, which serves as a starting point in the autumn sky.
walk.andromedaStep2: From Alpheratz, the star at one corner of the Great Square of Pegasus, follow the chain of stars of Andromeda toward Mirach, then toward Mu Andromedae.
walk.andromedaStep3: Near Mu Andromedae, look a little to the side of the alignment: under a dark sky, M31 resembles a small elongated and diffuse glow. If you don't see it, choose a darker location and let your eyes adapt.
walk.andromedaTip: M31 is much easier under a dark sky, without a bright Moon or light pollution. It is especially well placed in the evening in autumn and early winter.
walk.winterHexStep1: Start with Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, then spot Rigel in Orion.
walk.winterHexStep2: Continue along the outline toward Aldebaran, with its orange look, then Capella, very bright higher in the sky.
walk.winterHexTip: This figure is mostly visible on winter evenings. The stars must be above the horizon and a clear sky helps a lot.
walk.springTriIntro: Three bright stars, in three different constellations, form a wide triangle easy to memorize.
walk.winterHexIntro: Six very bright stars draw a large outline in the winter sky. Betelgeuse lies inside this figure.
walk.winterHexStep3: Continue toward Pollux, then Procyon, before returning to Sirius: you have traced the great winter hexagon.
walk.springTriStep1: Spot Arcturus, a very bright orange star, by extending the arc of the Big Dipper's handle.
walk.springTriStep2: Find Regulus in Leo to close the triangle: Arcturus, Spica and Regulus are the three vertices.
walk.springTriTip: The spring triangle is especially notable in spring and early summer in the northern hemisphere.
walk.dipperToArcturusTitle: From the Big Dipper to Arcturus
walk.dipperToArcturusIntro: The Big Dipper's handle allows you to find two bright stars: Arcturus then Spica. It is a classic landmark for learning the spring sky.
walk.dipperToArcturusStep1: Spot the two stars on the edge of the Big Dipper, Merak and Dubhe.
walk.dipperToArcturusStep2: Follow the curve of the handle to Alkaid, then extend the arc to find Arcturus, bright and orange.
walk.dipperToArcturusStep3: Continue in the same direction to reach Spica, in Virgo. The classic mnemonic is 'arc to Arcturus, spike to Spica'.
walk.dipperToArcturusTip: The path is especially handy in spring. The line is an approximate guide, not an exact trajectory.

universe.milkyWayPointer: ✦ Our position in the Milky Way
universe.descSolar: The Solar System spans about 100 astronomical units (AU) in this educational frame. One AU is the average Earth–Sun distance, about 149.6 million kilometres. The eight planets orbit the Sun, but distances are too large to be faithfully represented at this scale.
universe.noteSolar: Chosen frame: about 100 AU, i.e. 14.96 billion kilometres. The edge of the Solar System depends on what is considered (planetary orbits, distant regions or the Sun’s influence); the drawing remains schematic.
universe.descNearby: The Sun belongs to a neighbourhood of stars. Proxima Centauri, the closest known star after the Sun, lies about 4.24 light-years away. Distances between stars far exceed the dimensions of planetary systems.
universe.noteNearby: Stars are drawn to be visible; their sizes and spacings are schematic.
universe.descMilkyWay: The Sun lies in the disc of the Milky Way, in the local arm called the Orion Arm, about 26,000 light-years from the galactic centre. The galaxy contains hundreds of billions of stars.
universe.noteMilkyWay: Schematic top view: spiral arms are complex structures, not fixed rails.
universe.descLocalGroup: The Milky Way is part of the Local Group, a set of dozens of galaxies dominated by the Milky Way and the Andromeda galaxy. Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away.
universe.noteLocalGroup: Sizes and distances between galaxies are compressed to fit the view.
universe.descCosmicWeb: At very large scale, galaxies group into clusters and organize into filaments separated by immense voids. The Universe is about 13.8 billion years old. As space expanded while light travelled, the diameter of the observable Universe is today estimated at about 93 billion light-years.
universe.noteCosmicWeb: Didactic diagram, not a real or to-scale map: filaments and clusters are deliberately spaced to make the structure readable.
universe.scaleLocalGroup: Local Group · scale of several galaxies

constellation.intro: Choose a figure: the main stars, its drawing then its remarkable landmarks will be presented step by step.
constellation.tip: Start by spotting the brightest stars of the figure; not all of their names are common.
constellation.Cas: Look for a W or M made of five bright stars; its orientation varies with time and season.
constellation.UMa: First spot the seven stars of the Big Dipper: the edge opposite the handle helps find Polaris.
constellation.UMi: The Little Dipper forms a small saucepan; Polaris is at the end of its handle.
constellation.Ori: Look for the three almost aligned stars of the Belt, then the four stars that draw the hunter's body.
constellation.Lyr: Spot Vega, very bright, then the small parallelogram of stars that accompanies it.
constellation.Cyg: Follow the large cross of the Northern Cross: Deneb marks one end and Albireo the other.
constellation.Sco: Look for Antares, a reddish star, then follow the long curve that evokes the Scorpion's tail.
constellation.walkTip: First spot the brightest star, then slowly follow the golden strokes from one star to the next. Compare the figure to the map, taking into account its orientation in the sky.
